summary: The search warrant for defendant's residence was facially valid and sufficiently particular, and the motion court properly denied suppression without a hearing. Defendant's separate challenge to the manner of execution was unpreserved.

For grand larceny based on credit card theft, the statutory definition of credit card includes an account number, not just the physical card. The evidence was therefore legally sufficient even without proof that defendant possessed the tangible card.

Viewing the record in the light most favorable to the People, the evidence was legally sufficient for a rational jury to find that justification was disproved beyond a reasonable doubt. The conviction was affirmed.

Although police had probable cause to search defendant and his residence, the warrant and supporting materials did not establish probable cause to search two vehicles outside the home. Suppression of evidence from the vehicles was proper.

A late-disclosed witness statement did not satisfy Brady materiality on this record because there was no reasonable possibility of a different result. The Court reversed the Appellate Division's contrary ruling and remitted.

The record supported denial of a third CPL article 730 competency examination, and alleged prosecutorial misconduct was harmless in light of overwhelming proof. The trial court's denial of a last-minute adjournment request was also within discretion.

Executive Law 552's grant of concurrent prosecutorial authority to a gubernatorial special prosecutor was held unconstitutional as an improper transfer of district attorney power. The indictments obtained under that authority were not reinstated.
Any assumed evidentiary error was harmless because proof of guilt remained overwhelming and there was no reasonable possibility the challenged evidence affected the verdict. The order was affirmed.

The Appellate Term could not impose an extra-statutory special-circumstances bar on reprosecution after dismissal of a simplified traffic information for late supporting deposition service. Under Nuccio and the CPL, a new facially sufficient accusatory instrument was permissible.

Defendant's claim of presumptive vindictive sentencing after a successful appeal was unpreserved because no specific constitutional objection or plea-withdrawal motion was made. The sentence issue did not qualify for the illegal-sentence exception.

On these facts, the trial court did not abuse its discretion by excluding proposed adolescent-brain-development expert testimony offered to support a justification defense. The conviction was affirmed.

Use of translators in preparing supporting depositions from limited-English-proficiency witnesses did not create a hearsay defect that rendered the accusatory instruments facially insufficient. The challenged informations were upheld.
A valid negotiated appeal waiver barred review of defendant's CPL 380.50 allocution-at-sentencing claim under the circumstances presented. The order was affirmed.

Default judgments entered in traffic-infraction prosecutions after defendants failed to appear for trial were not authorized under the governing criminal procedure statutes in these circumstances. The Appellate Term's resolution was affirmed.

The People failed to establish that a warrantless backpack search was a valid search incident to arrest because the record did not show the bag was in defendant's immediate control. The case was remitted for consideration of unresolved alternative arguments.

For CPL article 700 purposes, an eavesdropping warrant is executed where authorized officers intentionally intercept communications, not where target phones are physically located. A Kings County justice therefore had authority to issue these warrants.

The vehicle stop was unsupported because the People failed at the suppression hearing to establish the reliability and basis of knowledge for the 911 tip. Suppression was required and the indictment was dismissed.

Defendant's right to counsel was violated when defense counsel was excluded from one of the People's psychiatric examinations after CPL 250.10 notice. The resulting error was not harmless, requiring a new trial.

County Court did not abuse its discretion in summarily denying the CPL 440.10 motion without a hearing because defendant's submissions did not sufficiently establish prejudice or entitlement to relief.

The trial court should have held a Rodriguez hearing before allowing the challenged identification evidence based only on prosecutorial assurances of witness familiarity. The case was remitted for Rodriguez/Wade proceedings as needed.
As the People conceded, the accusatory instrument failed to allege sufficient facts establishing a qualifying threat under Penal Law 240.30 (1) (a). The instrument was dismissed.

Grand jury proof was legally insufficient on mens rea for second-degree manslaughter in an overdose case: the evidence did not show defendant was aware of, or failed to perceive, a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death beyond general drug danger. The manslaughter count was dismissed.
New York City's Right of Way Law (Administrative Code 19-190) was upheld against due-process and state-law preemption challenges. The convictions were affirmed.
Defendant was deprived of the constitutional right to counsel when required to proceed through trial without counsel in circumstances not cured by standby/advisory counsel. A new trial was ordered.

The suppression court properly denied defendant's suppression motion without a hearing where the motion papers contained insufficient sworn factual allegations, including inadequate factual pleading of standing.

The record supported the lower courts' finding of founded suspicion to conduct a canine sniff of the vehicle exterior during the traffic stop, placing the issue beyond further review. The order was affirmed.

The trial court did not abuse discretion by precluding the proposed false-confession expert under the record presented and by denying eyewitness-identification expert testimony in light of corroborating proof. The conviction was affirmed.
Displaying statutory text on a visualizer during readback of supplemental jury instructions did not require party consent under CPL 310.30. The order was affirmed.

Because the sentencing court failed to make the required on-the-record youthful-offender eligibility determination for an armed-felony youth, remittal was required for proper consideration under Middlebrooks and Lofton.

Counsel's failure to raise a repugnancy challenge was not ineffective assistance where the issue was not clear-cut and dispositive given the charge. The Appellate Division order was reversed and remitted for unresolved issues.

Under the totality of the circumstances and the People's concession, defendant's appeal waiver was invalid and did not foreclose appellate review of the harsh-and-excessive sentence claim. The matter was remitted for further proceedings.

The Appellate Division erred as a matter of law by concluding there was no evidence linking defendant to the homicide despite DNA and related circumstantial proof. Its legal-sufficiency and weight analyses were reversed and the case remitted.

A challenge to SORA certification first raised on appeal was unpreserved, and the illegal-sentence exception did not apply because certification is not part of the criminal sentence. The Appellate Division order was reversed insofar as appealed from and remitted.

Questioning defendant about where he lived fell within the pedigree exception to Miranda under these circumstances, so suppression was properly denied on that ground. However, reversal and remittal were required because no Frye hearing was held on FST DNA statistical evidence.
Defendant's challenge to the sentencing court's consideration of portions of the presentence report was unpreserved, and no basis for relief was shown. The order was affirmed.

Under the unique voir dire circumstances, defendant's pre-waiver Antommarchi claim required a timely protest because he later waived appearance at sidebars and acquiesced after being invited to raise objections. The order was affirmed.

Defendant's claim that the CPL 400.21 predicate statement was deficient for omitting tolling periods was unpreserved and did not fit the narrow illegal-sentence exception. The Appellate Division order was reversed and remitted for unresolved issues.

Evidence was legally sufficient to sustain second-degree assault under accessorial liability because a rational factfinder could infer defendant shared a community of purpose with the assailants. The order was affirmed.

Sex trafficking under Penal Law 230.34 requires a link between advancing/profiting from prostitution and the enumerated coercive acts. A supplemental jury instruction improperly severed that link, so the sex-trafficking convictions were vacated and a new trial ordered on those counts, while the promoting-prostitution conviction remained.
